name: Greeny Blue
lede: Greeny Blue is a hedged color word: a blue that leans toward green, built with the suffix that English adds when it cannot quite commit to a shade.

sections.title: The -y suffix
sections.body:
Paterson explains the ending directly: -y can be added to a color to show hesitancy about the exact shade, as in browny or yellowy, and "greeny-blue" is his example [1]. He contrasts it with greenish-blue, which he says reads more like a noun [1]. So the name is a statement of doubt, not a standard.

The dictionary then uses it to define other names loosely: Adam blue is a greeny blue, grotto is a strong greeny-blue and French blue is a greeny-blue, sometimes purplish [2][3][4]. The same label covers colors that differ a lot, which is why it never became a fixed color.

sections.title: Greeny blues in cloth
sections.body: Balfour-Paul describes wealthier households hung with soft blue or greeny-blue draperies and tapestries, in a passage on woad [5]. Compare [[turquoise]], [[teal]] and [[sea-green]] for named greeny blues.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is rare in our archive: 6 of 23,781 paintings (0.03%, as photographed), rarer than 82% of the named colors [6]. The within-painting lens finds it in only 2 [6], so no pattern is safe to claim. These are photographs of varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test.
